title: Up the mountain (Matthew 5:1–2)
hook: he sits down, the way a rabbi teaches, and opens his mouth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the close of camp four, back to Galilee, and your line was: start again knowing more. What did you see in something familiar? Now camp five: the depths. Day two hundred thirty-two.

Think about how you can tell a talk is about to matter. The speaker stops pacing. Pulls up a chair. Sits down. Everyone leans in. For the next six weeks we're going somewhere new: the Sermon on the Mount, chapters five, six and seven of Matthew's Gospel. It's the longest block of Jesus's teaching in the Bible, and probably the most quoted. Blessed are the meek. Turn the other cheek. Salt and light. The Lord's Prayer. Treasure where moth and rust corrupt. The house on the rock. Words people use without knowing where they come from. And Matthew sets the scene in just two verses.
screen: `SOMEONE SITS DOWN; EVERYONE LEANS IN.` → `MATTHEW 5 TO 7.` → `WORDS EVERYONE QUOTES.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in the King James Bible: "And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him: And he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying." Three small details, and each one is doing something. First, he went up into a mountain. Matthew's first readers, many of them Jewish, would think of another teacher who went up a mountain: Moses on Sinai, receiving the law. Matthew seems to want that echo. Here's a new teacher on a mountain, giving teaching about how to live. Matthew never names the mountain. Tradition places it on a hillside above the Sea of Galilee, near Capernaum, and a church stands there today. Second, when he was set: when he sat down. Today a speaker stands to show authority. In his world, a teacher sat. Jesus sits down in the synagogue at Nazareth to teach, and he later speaks of teachers who sit in Moses' seat. Sitting down means: class is in session. Third, he opened his mouth. It sounds redundant; how else would he speak? But it's an old, solemn way of saying, what follows is weighty. It's like saying, and he began. Luke has a shorter version of some of the same teaching, set on a level place, and many readers think both gospels are gathering sayings Jesus taught many times. Either way, the posture is the point. Before the disciples hear a single word, they come close. The first move of the whole sermon isn't doing anything. It's coming near and listening.
screen: `HE WENT UP INTO A MOUNTAIN.` · `WHEN HE WAS SET: HE SAT DOWN.` · `HE OPENED HIS MOUTH.` · `THE DISCIPLES CAME NEAR.` · then, large: `AND HE OPENED HIS MOUTH, AND TAUGHT THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit down to listen. Wherever you are, sit, if you're not already. Let your feet rest on the ground. Put your phone face down. For these two minutes, you're not going to answer anything, fix anything or plan anything. Just listen: to the room, to your breath, to what's underneath the noise. If you pray, you can come near, the way the disciples did, and let God speak first. The bell holds the time.
Up the mountain. Where Jesus sits down, the way a teacher did, to begin the Sermon on the Mount.
Your line: sit down, listen. Today, in one conversation, sit down for it, if you can, and let the other person finish before you say a word. Day two hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Christians read the Sermon on the Mount often; many churches hear parts of it through the year, and some Christians read all three chapters at once, slowly, as a whole.

fork.setup: you're one of the disciples. a crowd is gathering, and Jesus goes up the hillside and sits down. what do you do?
fork.reveal: "when he was set, his disciples came unto him." the sermon begins with coming near and listening.

original.note: Greek: mountain, hill. Matthew 5:1, he went up into a mountain. hence orography, the study of mountains.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Sermon on the Mount was a speech to a crowd.
what it means: Jesus sits down, as a teacher did, and his disciples come near, with the crowds listening.
what a scholar hears: Matthew's mountain echoes Moses on Sinai; Luke 6 sets similar sayings on a level place.

notes: Camp open: camp five, the depths; part open: the Sermon on the Mount (days 232–261).
The Moses/Sinai echo is a widely held reading of Matthew; phrased as 'Matthew seems to want that echo'. Confirm.
Mount of Beatitudes near Capernaum/Tabgha, with a 20th-century church: 'a church stands there today'. Confirm.
'He opened his mouth' as a solemn idiom: a common commentary claim; confirm.
Relationship of Matthew 5–7 and Luke 6 is presented without choosing a theory.
